_note: Card text for palace objects with no Moves move: a short title and a deeper text. Objects with moves take their titles and deeper layers from the Moves page at build time. 'measured' quotes the module README or its results files only.

00a-4.title: The fit is a shadow
00a-4.text: Least squares picks the weights whose predictions lie closest to the targets. The predictions can only be mixes of the feature columns, so the best fit is the foot of a perpendicular from the target onto that space, and the residual stands at a right angle to every column. Gradient descent reaches the same foot step by step, but only while the step size stays below a bound set by the largest eigenvalue of the loss's curvature, 2XᵀX/n; past it every step overshoots further than the last.

00b-2.title: Each feature votes alone
00b-2.text: Naive Bayes models each class with one bell curve per feature and multiplies them, as if the features were independent once the class is known. That gives a closed form, trained in one pass over the data. When features move together, as in a tilted cloud, the product counts the same evidence twice, and the straight cut it gives cannot follow the tilt of the clouds.

00b-5.title: Centres walk to their points
00b-5.text: k-means sums a cloud up with k centres. Assign each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to the mean of its points, and repeat until nothing moves. Each round lowers the total squared distance, so it stops, but where it stops depends on where the centres started. Updating centres by a moving average over small batches adds noise that can shake one out of a poor spot.

00c-1.title: The widest plank
00c-1.text: A hard-margin support vector machine finds the line with the widest empty band between the classes. Written in its dual form, the solution is a weighted sum of training points, and only the points that touch the band get a weight α above zero. Those are the support vectors: remove any other point and the line does not move.
00c-1.formula: w = Σ αᵢ yᵢ xᵢ   (αᵢ > 0 only on the margin)

00c-2.title: Lift, then cut flat
00c-2.text: Two rings, one inside the other, cannot be split by a line. Add a third coordinate, x² + y², and the inner ring sits lower than the outer one, so a flat plane splits them. (This picture-book lift belongs to the kernel aᵀb + ‖a‖²‖b‖²; the module's quadratic kernel (aᵀb)² uses (x₁², √2·x₁x₂, x₂²).) The kernel trick never builds the new coordinates: the method only needs inner products, and a kernel function gives the inner product in the lifted space straight from the original points.

00c-3.title: Memories are valleys
00c-3.text: A Hopfield network stores patterns in its weights so that each one is a low point of an energy. Updating one unit at a time never raises the energy, so a damaged pattern rolls downhill into the stored one nearest to it. Store too many and the valleys merge: the classic network holds about 0.138 patterns per unit.

03-4.title: Out exactly as it came in
03-4.text: Byte-level BPE starts from the 256 byte values, so every string can be written, whatever its language or symbols. Encoding applies the learned merges; decoding joins the pieces back into bytes. Nothing is dropped or normalised on the way, so decoding an encoding gives the original text, byte for byte. The module tests that round trip in Python; its Zig trainer is checked to learn the identical list of merges.

03-5.title: Some languages pay more
03-5.text: Fertility is the number of tokens a tokenizer spends per word. A tokenizer trained mostly on English text learns long English pieces and cuts other languages finer, so the same message costs more tokens, more compute and more context in some languages than in others.
03-5.measured: SmolLM3's tokenizer: on pangrams, 1.14 tokens per word in English and 1.97 in Spanish (1.72×); on five ordinary sentence pairs, 58 tokens against 79 (1.36×) (results/fertility.json), module 03.

08-1.title: One stamp, every place
08-1.text: A convolution slides a small grid of weights over the image and writes one weighted sum at each position. The same weights are used everywhere, and each output sees only a small patch. Those two choices, sharing and locality, are why a convolutional network needs far fewer weights than a dense layer on the same image.

08-2.title: Detectors nobody drew
08-2.text: Train a small convolutional network to classify images and look at its first layer of kernels. They start as noise and end as edge detectors at several angles and as small blobs, much like the filters image processing used to design by hand. Nothing in the loss asks for edges; they are what helps.

08-4.title: Where the model looks
08-4.text: A vision transformer adds a [CLS] token whose final state is used to classify. Its attention weights in the last layer show which patches it reads most. Attention rollout multiplies the attention maps of every layer, with the residual path added in, to follow the flow from the input. Both are pictures of attention, not proofs of what caused the answer.

08-5.title: Pictures meet captions
08-5.text: CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder together so that a picture and its caption land close in one shared space. To classify with no task training, write one caption per class, such as "a photo of a dog", and pick the caption nearest the image. A model fine-tuned on the task can still beat it on that task.

05-1.title: Where the weights live
05-1.text: Walk a real model's modules and add up the tensors by role. The layout is module 04's block repeated: norm, attention, add, norm, MLP, add. Most parameters sit in the MLPs, fewer in attention, and the embedding table, shared with the output head, holds the rest; the norms are almost nothing.
05-1.measured: SmolLM2-360M, 361.8M parameters in 32 layers: about two thirds MLP, ~22% attention, ~13% embedding table (results/anatomy.json), module 05.

05-5.title: Read every layer's guess
05-5.text: The logit lens takes the hidden state after each layer and pushes it through the final norm and output head, as if the model stopped there. Early layers give junk; at some layer the right token reaches the top and stays. That layer is the decision layer. The lens reads early layers in the last layer's terms, which they do not use, so the junk means little.
05-5.measured: "The Eiffel Tower is located in the city of": ␣Paris reaches rank 1 at layer 27 of 32 and ends at 98.5% (results/logit_lens.json), module 05.

05-6.title: The envelope around each turn
05-6.text: A chat model was trained on conversations written in one exact format: special tokens mark where each turn starts and ends and who is speaking. The chat template writes your messages into that format. Leave it out, or use another model's, and the model sees text in a form it was not trained on; the template also adds text you never wrote.

07-1.title: One long scroll of numbers
07-1.text: A model file can be one flat run of bytes plus a manifest that says, for each tensor, its name, shape, type and where it starts. Loading is reading the manifest and pointing at the right bytes. The module's Zig engine loads a GPT this way, with no framework.

07-3.title: Prefill, then decode
07-3.text: Prefill pushes the prompt through the model to fill the cache. A GPU engine does it in one masked pass, every position attending to the ones before it; the module's Zig engine steps the prompt token by token. Decode then adds one token at a time. The new token comes last, so every earlier position is allowed: the mask has nothing to hide in its row, and with the cache only that one row is computed.

07-4.title: Trim the bag, then draw
07-4.text: Sampling turns the model's scores into one token. Temperature divides the scores before the softmax: below 1 it sharpens the odds, above 1 it flattens them. Top-k keeps only the k likeliest tokens; top-p keeps the smallest set whose odds add up to p. Renormalise what is left, then draw.

07-5.title: Fewer shades of ink
07-5.text: Quantising to int8 stores each weight as one of 255 levels, −127 to 127, plus a scale per row or block, a quarter of the size of float32. GGUF's Q8_0 does the same in blocks of 32; Q4_K goes down to about 4.5 bits a weight. The cost is rounding error, so measure quality before and after, the same way, on the same text.

07-6.title: Two scribes, one page
07-6.text: A hand-written engine is only right if it matches a trusted reference. Feed the same input to both, compare the outputs value by value, and fail the test if any value differs by more than a tolerance chosen for the number type. The module checks its Zig engine against PyTorch this way.

18-1.title: A gate on the satchel
18-1.text: A GRU keeps one state vector. At each token it proposes a candidate state and computes an update gate z between 0 and 1 for each unit. The new state is a mix: keep z of the old, take 1 − z of the candidate. Near 1 the unit holds on to what it had; near 0 it rewrites.

18-3.title: A recurrence that is a convolution
18-3.text: If the state update is linear and its decay does not depend on the input, the state after t tokens is a fixed weighted sum of the inputs: a convolution with a decaying kernel. A convolution can be computed for all positions at once, so it trains in parallel, and it must give the same numbers as stepping one token at a time.

18-4.title: When the gate decides
18-4.text: Mamba makes the decay depend on the token: the model chooses, per input, how much to keep. That selection is what lets it remember some tokens and skip others, but the kernel is no longer fixed, so the convolution trick is gone. A scan, which can still be split into parallel pieces, computes the chain instead.

18-5.title: A pile against a satchel
18-5.text: A transformer keeps every past token's keys and values, so its memory grows with each token it writes. A recurrent model carries one state of fixed size, so its memory per token stays flat however long the text. The module counts both and measures them.

27-1.title: A matrix that answers
27-1.text: A linear-attention model keeps its memory as a matrix S. To store a value v under a key k, add the outer product v kᵀ; to read, multiply S by a key. If the keys are orthogonal unit vectors, S k gives back exactly the value stored under k.
27-1.formula: S ← S + v kᵀ   ·   read: S k

27-2.title: Chalk over chalk
27-2.text: Linear attention only adds. Once more pairs are written than the state has dimensions, the keys cannot all be orthogonal, and each read returns its value plus a little of every other. Decay multiplies S by α before each write, so old pairs fade and new ones read cleaner, at the price of forgetting.

27-4.title: Correct, and wipe a little
27-4.text: The gated delta rule combines both ideas: decay the whole state by α, then write by correcting what it returns for k. Run token by token it is a slow loop, so the module computes it a chunk at a time: within a chunk the corrections depend on each other through a triangular system, solved in one go.
27-4.formula: S ← α S − β (α S k − v) kᵀ

27-5.title: How many names a slate holds
27-5.text: Write n pairs of random unit vectors into a 32 × 32 state and read every key back. A read counts as right when it lies closer to its own value than to any other. At 8 pairs every rule reads nearly all back. By 32 only plain adding still does (0.99); the rules that forget have slipped to 0.81, 0.75 and 0.56.
27-5.measured: Recall at 64 pairs: linear 0.83, delta 0.47, decay (α = 0.95) 0.40, gated delta 0.28; mean of 20 draws, random keys, module 27.

09-4.title: Fewer, longer strides
09-4.text: DDPM removes noise in many small random steps. DDIM uses the same trained network but takes larger, deterministic steps that skip most of the schedule. Fewer steps run faster; past some point the samples lose detail. In the diffusers library this is a change of scheduler, not a new model.

09-5.title: A whispered word steers
09-5.text: Stable Diffusion denoises in the small latent space of an autoencoder, not in pixels, and feeds a text encoding into the denoiser. Classifier-free guidance runs the denoiser with and without the text and pushes the step further in the direction the text adds. A larger guidance scale follows the prompt more closely and gives less varied images.

33-1.title: Straight strings, one step
33-1.text: Flow matching joins each noise sample to a data sample by a straight line and trains a network to predict the velocity along it. Sampling follows those velocities from noise to data in several steps. In one step the best guess for any noise point is the average of every data point it could be heading to, so a one-step sample lands in the middle.
33-1.formula: xₜ = (1 − t) x₀ + t x₁   ·   target: x₁ − x₀

33-3.title: The step dial
33-3.text: A masked diffusion model can fill a line in any number of steps. With many steps it reveals a few characters at a time, each one chosen knowing the others; with few steps it must fill many blanks at once, each guessed as if the others were still blank, and the line gets worse. Which blanks fill first, the surest or random ones, changes the result too.

33-4.title: Board by board
33-4.text: Block diffusion writes a line in short blocks from left to right. Inside a block it denoises like a masked diffusion model; finished blocks are fixed and kept in a KV cache, as in module 07, so each new block reads them without recomputing. It sits between writing left to right and filling everything at once.

33-5.title: Who wins on repeated data
33-5.text: Train both objectives on the same small text, seen again and again. The left-to-right twin learns fast, reaches its best held-out loss, then overfits. The diffusion model starts slowly and keeps improving long after. Where the curves cross is not a win: the twin stopped at its best epoch is still ahead.
33-5.measured: 100,000 characters: twin best at epoch 64 (2.287), held-out 2.538 at epoch 200; diffusion bound 2.498 at epoch 200 and still falling; module 33.
